#7733. Pactiv Evergreen settles for $6.25M over 2023 North Carolina mill closure

The restitution amount is more than half of what Pactiv Evergreen received from the state in economic development grants for the site.

The paper mill in Canton had been in operation for more than 100 years prior to then-owner Pactiv shutting it down in 2023, according to the state of North Carolina. Blue Ridge Paper Products operated the facility since 1999, and in 2007 that company became Evergreen Packaging through a merger. Pactiv Evergreen formed in 2020 through the combination of Evergreen Packaging and Pactiv, both of which were previously acquired by Reynolds Group Holdings.

At the time of the Canton mill’s closure, many people expressed surprise at Pactiv Evergreen’s decision. The company made the announcement in March 2023 along with other closure and restructuring disclosures, and CEO Mike King noted a “challenging market environment” for Pactiv’s beverage merchandising business. North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper said in a statement last week that the Canton closure came as a “gut punch" to the local and state economies.

Upon introducing the lawsuit in May 2024, then-Attorney General Josh Stein noted that taxpayers “invested in Pactiv Evergreen to bolster our state’s economy,” but Pactiv didn’t hold up its end of the bargain. He said at the time that his office had tried working with Pactiv for a year to address the company’s obligations, but it had “become clear that legal action was necessary to hold Pactiv accountable.” The initial lawsuit sought repayment of the full $12 million in economic incentives that Pactiv had received.

The settlement should not be viewed as an admission to wrongdoing, according to the North Carolina Department of Justice.

“Pactiv broke its promise to the state and the people of Canton, and today’s settlement holds it accountable for violating its agreement,” Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who was elected in November and took office last month, said of the new settlement. “This settlement will allow the people of Canton and Haywood County to immediately put millions back into rebuilding their economy after the mill’s closure, and it will shield them from future litigation from Pactiv.”

The candidates for state attorney general repeatedly brought up the mill issues on the campaign trail prior to November’s election. Both candidates expressed a desire to hold Pactiv accountable.

Pactiv had filed a motion to dismiss the complaint in July 2024. But a judge denied that motion in October, allowing the lawsuit to proceed.

“We are pleased to have resolved with the State of North Carolina all outstanding matters relating to the closure and sale of our former Canton mill site. We thank our employees for their contributions to our company and wish the Canton community well in this next chapter for the Town,” said Pactiv Evergreen Tuesday in an emailed statement.

This wasn’t Pactiv’s first legal battle over the Canton site.

In autumn 2023, the company reached a settlement worth more than $2 million with the U.S. EPA over Clean Air Act violations at Canton. Earlier that year, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality said the site violated water quality requirements; the company denied the allegations. In 2021 and 2022, the mill faced state air quality violations.

Novolex is in the process of acquiring Pactiv Evergreen for $6.7 billion. The deal, which would take Pactiv private, is expected to close during the first half of this year.

#7732. Judge deals new setback to Trump arch plans

Officials in Arlington County, Va., contend the arch would pose various nuisances and hazards and that the plans for it are illogical.

ALEXANDRIA, Va. (CN) â Describing President Donald Trump’s plans for a 250-foot arch near the capital as “such a rushed job” in a ruling from the bench on Friday, U.S. District Court Judge Leonie Brinkema slapped his administration with a preliminary injunction halting construction.

The National Park Service, which would oversee the project, “has not analyzed the potential impacts,” said Brinkema, a Bill Clinton appointee. She pointed to the hazard of cranes, which could rise more than 320 feet in a region with notable helicopter traffic.

Brinkema also took issue with the administration’s claim to be fulfilling a 1925 statute authorizing the Memorial Bridge.

The law did not call for an arch but columns, local officials say. At the time, the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport hadn’t been built.

“There was no airport in sight,” the judge told Department of Justice lawyers. “This is a project without congressional approval.”

The case before Brinkema â brought by Arlington County officials â is one of four lawsuits opposing Trump’s proposed triumphal arch at Memorial Circle just outside Washington, D.C.

In a separate case, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Wednesday lengthened an order blocking the Trump administration from breaking groundÂ for the project through Dec. 3. Brinkema’s Friday injunction will further extend that order.

The Park Service is required to comply with the National Environmental Policy Act by closely examining the environmental impacts of the plans, county officials argue in their lawsuit.

That process obligates the government to consider how the project could harm the human environment â including historic, cultural and aesthetic impacts â and to evaluate reasonable alternatives and mitigation measures, county officials say. They complain the arch âwill dwarf Parisâs Arc de Triomphe and directly obstruct the sight line between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery that was deliberately created to symbolize the nationâs post-Civil War reunification.â

In their complaint, county officials also took issue with Trumpâs plans to have the arch serve as both tourist attraction and military site that would âhouse, store and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus snipers.â They contend the Park Service âfailed to consider the serious safety risks inherent igovernmentâs planned military installation," resulting in “a decision so illogical that it cannot be ascribed to mere differences in judgment.â

Beyond that, the county also argues that the arch will be a nuisance shouldered by the officials and populace of that county. They wrote: “The construction and continuing presence of the arch will severely impede the countyâs provision of emergency services to the immediate surrounding area, including Arlington National Cemetery; burden county infrastructure and law-enforcement efforts; and interfere with the countyâs planning and development efforts.â

Attorneys for the Department of Justice will appeal the decision, according to a department spokesman.

#7730. ‘The worst COP ever’: UN climate summit on brink of failure

Developing nations and activists are furious over a lack of pledges to phase out fossil fuels and boost climate funding in a draft declaration from this yearâs U.N. climate summit.Â

(CN) â With the United States a climate-denying no-show and the European Union retreating on climate leadership, the annual United Nations climate summit veered toward failure Friday.

The summit, known as COP31, was on the brink of becoming a massive disappointment with civil society groups calling it the worst U.N. climate summit in history and Panama’s negotiator saying the world was âbeing held hostage by the petroleum mafia.â

The two-week summit â held this year in Antalya, Turkey â formally ended Friday, but negotiations on the wording of a final declaration were set to stretch into the weekend.

Huge divisions opened up Thursday after richer nations, led by the European Union, offered paltry sums to help developing countries fight climate change and oil-producing countries managed to strip language about phasing out fossil fuels from a draft text of a final declaration.

âWithout any doubt, this has been the worst COP ever,â said Mohamed Adow, the head of Power Shift Africa, at a news conference Friday held by the Climate Action Network, a global civil society coalition.

Tasneem Essop, the executive director of Climate Action Network, said there was ânothing on the table that protects people or addresses the priorities of the Global South.â

Anger was directed at the EU for backing away from pledges to provide poorer countries with large sums of money to deal with climate change.

On the eve of the summit, Wopke Hoekstra, the EU’s climate commissioner, said new financial commitments were âdead in the water.â

âThink about that,â Essop, a South African, said. âDead in the water. For us in the Global South, dead in the water is very literal.â

By Friday, richer countries had pledged only about $50 million into a fund to help countries adapt to climate change.

But that amounted to only one-sixth of an annual target of $300 million agreed to at last year’s climate summit in BelÃ©m, Brazil, and fell well short of a broader goal to mobilize $1.2 billion from 2026 to 2029.

The EU rejected the criticism with its officials arguing the bloc provides the lionâs share of global climate finance. Last year, the EU and its 27 member states provided about $35 billion in public sources to support developing countries deal with climate change, according to an EU news release.

But developing nations blasted the lack of new commitments at the summit from wealthier countries.

âWe didnât come here to beg,â said Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, the lead negotiator for African nations. âWe came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries.â

Many delegates and activists blamed European countries for blocking progress in other areas too.

In recent years, the EU has backed away from leading on climate issues in the face of domestic backlash against its ambitious climate goals.

Europe’s retreat on climate stems from weak industrial output, the rise of far-right parties, a cost-of-living crisis and the climate skepticism of U.S. President Donald Trump.

For a second year in a row, the U.S. did not send a delegation to the climate summit, a move that severely undermined the talks.

Upon returning to the White House in 2025, Trump removed the U.S. from the 2015 Paris climate accord, and thereby withdrew one of the world’s top emitters from the international framework to reduce carbon emissions.

In Turkey, delegations and activists were dismayed at the removal of language calling for the phase-out of fossil fuels.

Instead, the draft declaration put emphasis on boosting electrification around the world and supporting technologies to remove carbon from the atmosphere.

The draft text called for increasing electricity’s share of global energy use from 23% to 35% by 2035. This pledge was almost certain to remain in the final text and become the summit’s main theme.

But even this pledge was criticized for not saying renewable energy sources should be favored over fossil fuels in this electrification drive.

The final text likely will include support for carbon capture and storage technology, but critics said it remains an unproven means of reducing greenhouse gases.

Australia and Turkey jointly presided over the negotiations and argued the summit had made progress.

Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister and summit co-president, said it was not necessary to call for a phase-out of fossil fuels because that language had been included in previous COP declarations. In 2023, a climate summit in Dubai called for phasing out fossil fuels, but since then the climate talks largely have avoided the topic.

âI do not think we are taking a step back,â Kurum said. âI think the determined steps we have taken need to be supported. It is clear we cannot get anywhere by repeating the same discussions.â

Courthouse News reporter Cain Burdeau is based in the European Union.

#7729. An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences. But the significant shift towards Democrats in states previously controlled by Republicans is likely to impact immigration law even sooner. The Supreme Court is currently considering whether to add to its calendar a case about the constitutionality of an immigration law enacted by Iowa in 2024. The justices had previously signaled their openness to weighing in, but the state’s Republican attorney general, who asked the court to hear the case, lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, casting doubt on the case’s future.

Iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct. For example, anyone who has previously been excluded or deported from the United States by federal immigration officials but “is at any time found” in Iowa can be convicted of an aggravated misdemeanor and imprisoned for up to two years. As an alternative to potential conviction, the law allows a state judge overseeing a criminal prosecution to order the defendant to leave the United States. Anyone who fails to leave as required can be convicted of a felony and imprisoned for as much as 10 years.

The state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act permits criminal prosecution of migrants who are found in the United States after having previously been removed. It also allows immigration judges to order a migrant to depart the United States. By resembling federal law, Senate File 2340’s proponents hoped to assist the federal government’s efforts to penalize and remove from the United States people who had violated federal immigration law.

In two separate lawsuits, challengers questioned the law’s constitutionality. An advocacy group based in Des Moines, the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, and two Iowa residents who had previously been removed from the United States filed one lawsuit, while the Justice Department, during President Joe Biden’s tenure, filed the other. In June 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa sided with the challengers in both cases. Since Senate File 2340 regulates immigration, it treads on an area of law that is the responsibility of the federal government, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher concluded. As the Supreme Court explained in a 2012 decision, Arizona v. United States, involving Arizona’s attempt to enact its own immigration laws, “The federal power to determine immigration policy is well settled.”

In addition, any time that Congress enacts legislation in an area in which it is authorized to do so, including immigration, the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution prioritizes federal law over state law. “Under this principle, Congress has the power to preempt state law,” the Supreme Court explained in Arizona. By enacting a detailed, complicated set of immigration laws, including criminal offenses related to migration, “Congress ‘left no room’ for state regulation” of migration, Locher explained. Since Senate File 2340 attempts to regulate migration, it is likely preempted. Locher thus blocked Iowa from enforcing it.

Within days, Iowa’s attorney general, Republican Brenna Bird, appealed the district court’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. While the case was pending before the 8th Circuit, President Trump returned to the White House, and the Justice Department asked the district court to dismiss its lawsuit. Despite the federal government’s shifting position, Senate File 2340 did not fare well before the 8th Circuit. Deciding Bird’s appeal of the case brought by the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two Iowa residents, the circuit court concluded that each section of Senate File 2340 conflicts with federal immigration law and is therefore likely preempted.

Having lost at the 8th Circuit, Bird asked the Supreme Court to weigh in. Iowa’s law should be allowed to go into effect because it merely “mirrors federal law,” Bird told the justices in her request for review last July. Unsurprisingly, Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two residents who challenged the law urged the justices not to add this case to their calendar. They argued that the 8th Circuit applied the law in line with other federal courts that have grappled with similar disputes, so the court’s intervention is unnecessary.

Last month, the justices signaled that they were more interested in this case, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, than most others vying for their attention. On Oct. 19, the court invited the solicitor general – the federal government’s top lawyer before the Supreme Court – to explain whether the Trump administration thinks the court should become involved. Calling for the solicitor general’s view is a key sign that the justices are closely considering whether to add the case to their calendar. Of the thousands of cases that the court is asked to review every year, the justices request the solicitor general’s view in a small handful – “around 10 or 11 times every term,” according to SCOTUSblog contributor John Elwood. For that reason, invitations to the solicitor general “serve as powerful signals that a petition has attracted the court’s serious attention,” Elwood explained.

The solicitor general has not yet responded to the court’s invitation, but there is reason to believe it will ask the court to grant Iowa’s request – or would have absent this month’s electoral swing. By voluntarily dismissing its lawsuit last year, the Trump administration removed the federal government from stopping Iowa’s enforcement of Senate File 2340. Since then, it has left no doubt that it stands with Iowa. After the 8th Circuit concluded that Iowa could not enforce the law, the Justice Department urged the full court to rehear the case and side with Iowa. “[T]he panel opinion misapplied preemption principles to affirm the district court’s preliminary injunction,” the Justice Department told the 8th Circuit in an amicus brief that it filed in the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice’s case.

But the results of this month’s elections may have dimmed the prospects of Supreme Court review. Bird lost her reelection bid to Democrat Nate Willems. Though Willems has not publicly taken a position on Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340, in an interview he accused her of having “filed too many of what I think of as political lawsuits.” He instead said he would focus on “times when there is a real threat to Iowans or a real harm,” and promised to boost the attorney general’s work on behalf of consumers, workers, and the environment. Willems’ Democratic colleague Rob Sand won the state’s gubernatorial election. Sand also has not publicly explained his position on Senate File 2340, but with Democrats holding two of the highest offices in state government, they are likely to align with each other.

Once sworn in as Iowa’s next attorney general, Willems will be able to move forward with or drop Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340. Under the court’s rules, a case will be dismissed when both parties agree. Since Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the state’s two residents who challenged the law have indicated that they do not want the court to intervene, all that is left is for Willems to make his view known. Having already lost in two courts, Senate File 2340 remains alive only thanks to Bird’s insistence that those judges misunderstood the state’s role in punishing migrants. But if he wants, Willems can turn the attorney general’s office’s attention to other matters, providing yet another reason why elections matter.

César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

#7728. What businesses should know about consent rules when calling consumers

Rules around obtaining consumer consent before calling or texting are in a state of legal and regulatory uncertainty – and companies should remain cautious.

Senosiain is an associate and Rollins is a shareholder at Gunster. Views are the authors’ own.

The Telephone Consumer Protection Act governs calls and text messages sent by businesses to consumers. One such rule is that businesses must obtain express written consent prior to sending text messages to consumers, if they are using an automated telephone dialing system or making calls using an artificial or pre-recorded voice, including the use of AI bots.

The TCPA also provides that businesses may not call or text consumers on the federal Do Not Call List unless prior express consent is given. Even basic telemarketing calls and text messages require prior express consent. Violation of the statute can trigger liability for up to $1,500 per call or text message sent.

Additionally, many states have their own version of the TCPA, deemed “mini-TCPAs,” that require compliance for all businesses who make calls to consumer-residents in that state, regardless of where the business is domiciled.

Many companies use lead generators which gather consumer consents for multiple businesses and then provide the companies with consent and contact information for those potential consumers. Lead generators who obtain proper written consent can be a very useful tool for companies. This was generally permissible under the TCPA.

However, in 2023, the Federal Communications Commission updated its TCPA rules requiring “one-to-one consent” which was to become effective Jan. 27, 2025.

The one-to-one consent rule provides that if a business uses an ATDS, artificial or prerecorded voice, the business must obtain prior express consent, one seller at a time.

Thus, it prevents lead generators from using a single consumer’s consent for multiple businesses. Additionally, the one-to-one consent rule provides that the consent must be clear and conspicuous, and the calls and texts initiated pursuant to the consent must be logically and topically associated with the interaction that prompted the consent. This rule applies to both text messages and phone calls.

On Jan. 24, 2025, the FCC postponed the 2023 order by a year, until Jan. 26, 2026. Later that same day the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the 2023 Order, thus eliminating the one-to-one consent rule.

The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals held “that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority under the TCPA because the 2023 Order’s new consent restrictions impermissibly conflict[ed] with the ordinary statutory meaning of prior express consent.”

Notably, the court ruled that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority at the outset, when it created the one-to-one consent rule. The court held that the 2023 Order’s one-to-one prior express consent restriction impermissibly conflicted with the ordinary statutory meaning of “prior express consent.” Thus, the Court vacated application of the 2023 Order, and remanded for further proceedings.

As a result, it is very likely that we will see other cases challenging TCPA regulations, especially as to the consent required before making a telemarketing call or text message using an ATDS.

It is unclear whether the FCC will revise its 2023 Order to comply with the Eleventh Circuit’s decision. In order to be prepared for this rule to come into effect, and in an abundance of caution, businesses who use lead generators to source potential consumers’ consent should ascertain that the lead generators are obtaining individual, one-to-one consent.

Businesses should also only contact consumers who provide this consent for telemarketing that is logically and topically associated with that which the consent was provided. Further, in addition to storing consumer contact information, businesses must retain the consent forms, information as to when consent was given, and through whom. Even businesses that do not use lead generators to obtain consent should continue to review their consent practices to ensure strict compliance with the TCPA and mini-TCPAs.

The TCPA requires prior express consent, and in many cases, prior express written consent, for calls and text messages made to prospective consumers. Regardless of any changes to the TCPA, the FTSA still requires that businesses obtain prior express written consent when making unsolicited telephone calls (including sending text messages) using an automated system. And lastly, to further protect your business, the consent form should have robust terms of service, including a class action waiver.

We continue to recommend that businesses ensure compliance with the TCPA, FTSA, and any other state regulations by always obtaining express written consent prior to contacting potential consumers via calls or text messages.

#7727. Markets tumble as AI bubble threatens to burst

Fears over artificial intelligence have come to a head, causing tech stocks to plunge and the Nasdaq to lose all its gains for the year in mere days.

MANHATTAN (CN) â Investors and economists have warned for weeks about an artificial intelligence bubble.

This weekâs sell-off may be the payoff to that prediction.

By the closing bell on Friday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 4,199 points and the S&P 500 fell 651 points, both verging on market corrections. The Nasdaq had a pretty bad week, too, falling 2,519 points.

Analysts warn the carnage may not be over.

âWe think the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 have further to run,â James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics, wrote in an investorâs note. “How this plays out within the stock market will depend on what is driving these falls.â

Earlier in the week, investors were temporarily pleased with Nvidiaâs positive earnings, which showed third-quarter revenue beat expectations by $6 billion and more than 100% higher than a year ago. Nvidiaâs revenue is also more than double what it was the same time in 2025, despite former CEO Jensen Huangâs scandalous departure last week.

Even with some calling for Huangâs return, the company seems well-poised to move on without him. âOur momentum is real,â interim CEO Colette Kress said in the companyâs earnings release. âOur roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.â

Not even the record-breaking initial public offering from Anthropic this week helped tech stocks, as shares of Anthropic fell more than 11% since its inception on Thursday.

Beyond tech stocks, other data this week showed mixed signals for the economy.

The monthly consumer sentiment survey from the University of Michigan increased slightly over October and now is roughly where it stood on November 2025. All of the surveyâs index components increased, with short-term expected business conditions increasing 13% over the last month and expectations for gas prices over the next year falling to their lowest reading since February.

âCurrent personal finances improved from last month for middle- and low-wealth consumers, who felt some relief stemming from recent declines in gas prices,â the surveyâs director Joanne Hsu said in a statement. âIn contrast, those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline, consistent with this monthâs agitation in stock markets.â

Not surprisingly, a growing number of respondents mentioned a potential AI bubble, as well as concerns about its effect on labor markets.

Retail sales came in roughly as expected, but the 0.2% increase in sales for October was far less than then 0.8% seen for September. Still, experts point to the report as evidence consumers are not afraid to keep spending.

The reason for the drop from September is likely due to the fall in gasoline station spending, since oil prices have come down in the last several weeks. Exclude autos and gasoline, though, and retail sales increased by 0.5% last month.

Other areas showed strength. Online spending and restaurant spending continue apace, at a 12% annualized increase and 7% annualized increase, respectively. Health and personal care stores also saw a 1.5% monthly gain in sales.

âAs long as consumers continue to spend and the economy keeps growing, then profits will grow as well, and markets will eventually find their footing and begin moving higher again,â said Chris Zacarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management.

Other data shows the economy slowing. The Empire State Manufacturing Survey showed an 18-point drop to 7.8, compared with the expectation it would drop only to 16. While the surveyâs general business conditions index remained positive at 7.8, it also fell slightly.

On the plus side, the surveyâs employment measure expanded at the fastest pace seen in more than four years. Respondent firms are more optimistic about economic conditions improving in the upcoming months.

#7726. Not Horsing Around: Carriage owners file lawsuit to challenge new ban in NYC

A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators. (Photo from Shutterstock)

A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.

The city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to sunset the carriages by June 1, 2028, in all five boroughs in the city. The union representing carriage operators and owners argues that their livelihood has been taken away and seeks to have the ban struck down.

“The city’s approach can be summarized in 12 words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” according to the suit.

Additionally, the new law stipulates the “humane disposition” of the horses. Animal rights activists have in the past expressed concern over the welfare of the horses. Earlier this year, an 18-year-old tourist died after jumping from a runaway carriage—the first fatality since the carriages were introduced into Central Park in New York City.

“Our city has changed, and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” Mamdani said.

#7724. The Supreme Court before it stood apart

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press)

In her excellent new book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history shows that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “umpire,” is not nearly as originalist as we tend to assume.

Shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

Shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different; except at certain prescheduled events, justices no longer directly communicate with the people in that circuit as part of their duties, but handle applications from it in the corridors of the marble palace. “Judicial representation” is most definitely no longer a thing.

But this just scratches the surface of the differences that Shelden lays out. In the 19th century, the justices were active participants in the political debates of their time, in ways that today would not only be grounds for profound criticism but even potential impeachment.

Chief Justice John Marshall was himself an active participant in such discourse. In 1800, before becoming chief, Marshall began contributing to the Washington Federalist, a newspaper established to support President John Adams and later oppose Thomas Jefferson. Marshall’s involvement was so extensive that he became known as the brains behind the paper. Nor did his appointment to the court entirely sever his connection to it. Elias Caldwell, the Supreme Court’s clerk during Marshall’s tenure, subsequently became its proprietor. The paper remained staunchly Federalist under Caldwell’s leadership, regularly attacking the Jefferson administration’s policies as unconstitutional.

Marshall’s political opponents suspected that he continued to exert considerable influence behind the scenes at the Washington Federalist even as chief justice, directing those attacks. Indeed, the Philadelphia Aurora, a newspaper aligned with Jefferson, described Caldwell as “a creature of John Marshall, chief justice.” Shelden casts doubt on Caldwell’s denial of Marshall’s involvement. And given that Caldwell was Marshall’s own clerk at the Supreme Court, you can understand the skepticism.

Justice William Johnson provides another example. In 1823, Johnson ruled (in his lower-court circuit-riding role) that South Carolina’s Negro Seamen Act, which authorized the detention of free Black sailors arriving in Charleston, violated the Constitution. Local officials were furious and refused to publish his opinion in the newspapers. So Johnson took his argument directly to the public, putting his opinion in a pamphlet that was circulated around the country, and then supporting the decision via pseudonymously authored op-eds that submitted his interpretation of the Constitution was correct.

Nor were the justices’ newspaper writings limited to defending their decisions. In 1848, Justice John McLean published letters addressing such political issues as the national bank, taxation, infrastructure, and the Mexican-American War, all while his supporters were encouraging him to pursue the presidency.

And in 1859, Justice John Catron publicly opposed proposed Tennessee legislation that would have enslaved free Black residents who remained in the state. Catron used his connections at the Nashville Union and American to publish a letter criticizing the legislation. The newspaper’s editors attacked his position, producing a public back-and-forth in its pages. Catron’s letter was even reprinted in Missouri, where similar legislation was under consideration. Tennessee ultimately rejected the proposal, and Shelden suggests Catron’s intervention may have mattered.

To put this in perspective, such actions would be akin to Justice Clarence Thomas writing an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal defending the Republican Party’s position on disputed legislation, or Justice Elena Kagan publishing an article in The New York Times supporting a Democratic president’s legislative agenda.

Yet the justices’ political involvement went well beyond expressing opinions publicly. Some actually ran for elected office while continuing to serve on the court.

Shelden recounts the example of Justice Smith Thompson, who accepted the nomination for governor of New York in 1828 while a justice. Thompson ultimately lost to Martin Van Buren by more than 30,000 votes. After losing the election, Thompson simply continued serving on the court, where he remained for another 15 years.

Justice McLean, meanwhile, was discussed as a potential presidential candidate in the 1830s, with political allies contemplating his nomination even as he continued hearing cases. Indeed, both McLean and his colleague, Justice Levi Woodbury, would later emerge as presidential contenders in 1848.

Justice William Johnson, appointed by President Thomas Jefferson, actually won election as a commissioner of the poor in Charleston Neck, South Carolina, in 1826. In this role, he exercised authority over local taxation, patronage, and public resources. Johnson held this elected position, and won reelection, while continuing to serve on the Supreme Court.

Again, by way of comparison, imagine Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson declaring herself a candidate for the 2028 presidential election – while continuing to decide cases and write opinions. Or contemplate Justice Neil Gorsuch simultaneously holding an elected local government office with taxing authority.

Just as notable was the willingness of justices to involve themselves directly in the work of the other branches of government. In doing so, they corresponded with presidents and members of Congress about public policy. They even offered advice on legislation and, in some instances, helped craft it.

During Reconstruction, Chief Justice Salmon Chase pressed President Andrew Johnson on Black suffrage and used his political relationships to influence Reconstruction policy. For his part, just a few years earlier, Justice John Campbell of Alabama sought to influence President-elect Lincoln to issue a public statement reassuring Southern moderates that his administration would not interfere with slavery in their states. Campbell even offered to publish a letter in his own name, as a citizen of Alabama, to help create an occasion for Lincoln to make such a statement.

When Lincoln declined to act, Campbell turned to President James Buchanan. He urged Buchanan to send commissioners to the secession conventions to persuade the delegates to preserve the Union. Campbell’s efforts ultimately failed. But consider what he was doing: a sitting Supreme Court justice was privately advising both an incoming and an outgoing president about how to address the most consequential political crisis in the nation’s history.

Now imagine Chief Justice John Roberts privately consulting with President Donald Trump about birthright citizenship, or Justice Sonia Sotomayor advising former President Joe Biden about his unconstitutional student loan forgiveness program and how it could be fixed.

In the dénouement of the book, Shelden traces how the political world of the justices changed as the 19th century drew to a close. Circuit riding ended, the legal profession grew more formal, and the court became more centered in Washington. As the country marked the Constitution’s centennial, lawyers and judges helped tell a new story of the court, one that made political detachment seem like some sort of longstanding tradition. (To be fair, this did not bring such political involvement to an immediate end.)

If I have one criticism of Shelden’s otherwise excellent work, it is that she doesn’t explore this transformation in nearly the same depth as she does the earlier history. How, exactly, did the justices (and their fellow Americans) come to accept a view of the court so different from the one they had held for much of the 19th century, and which we hold today? That is a fascinating question in its own right, and perhaps the worthy subject of a follow-up volume.

Regardless, Shelden’s history offers a challenge to today’s justices, as well as to proponents and critics of the modern court. Nineteenth-century justices participated much more freely in political life, while today’s justices insist that they must stand apart from politics, even as many Americans cast a dubious side eye upon that claim. Was it better when justices did not deny the political world they inhabited and were a part of? And can the way we look at the court, and the way the justices see themselves, change again? I don’t think the answers are obvious. But Shelden’s book made clear to me that a reflexive dismissal of such questions is based more on historical ignorance than any fixed tradition of the Supreme Court as appearing apolitical.

Mark Miller directs Environment and Natural Resources litigation at Pacific Legal Foundation

Recommended Citation: Mark Miller, The Supreme Court before it stood apart, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 18, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-supreme-court-before-it-stood-apart/

MANHATTAN (CN) â A New York City judge on Friday refused to block the rollout of Democrat Mayor Zohran Mamdaniâs campaign promise to open five city-operated supermarkets that sell pantry staples at a 30% discount.

A group of Harlem and Bronx grocers, led by the National Supermarket Association, sued the city in September, claiming five tax-funded supermarkets, one in each borough, would use predatory pricing to drive independent competitors out of business. They asked U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon to temporarily block the city from selecting operators for the stores.

Rochon, a Joe Biden appointee, denied the preliminary injunction Friday, finding the grocers failed to establish grounds for the injunctive relief based on attempted monopolization.

âThe heart of the dispute, however, lies in plaintiffsâ ability to meet the second prerequisite: a dangerous probability of recoupment. Plaintiffs cannot make that showing here,â she wrote, referring to the likelihood that the stores could recover losses from below-cost pricing by later charging inflated monopoly prices after weakening competitors.

âGiven defendantsâ lack of a profit incentive, and the lack of any evidence that the stores will be permitted to raise prices to a supracompetitive level in the future given the structure of N.Y.C Groceries, the court concludes that plaintiffs have not shown a âdangerous probabilityâ of recoupment,â she wrote.

Without a recoupment prerequisite, Rochon wrote, the existing grocery stores âeffectively seek to flatten predatory pricing claims to impose liability if a government actor intervenes in a private market resulting in prices below average variable cost.â

âSuch a rule would undermine the federal antitrust laws that exist to promote consumer welfare,â she wrote.

Richard Lawson, vice-chair of litigation at America First Policy Institute, said Friday the plaintiffs intend to move forward with the case and âwill be reviewing our options in light of the denied motion for preliminary injunction.â

âWhile we are disappointed by todayâs ruling, our concerns about the consequences of taxpayer-subsidized grocery stores on New York Cityâs independent grocers remain unchanged,â he wrote in a statement on the ruling.

Lawson argued at a hearing last week that the cityâs taxpayer-funded 30% discount mandate violates federal antitrust laws against predatory pricing.

The first stores are planned for East Harlem and Hunts Point in the Bronx. The Bronx location, at the former Spofford Juvenile Detention Facility, is expected to open next year, no later than the end of 2027.

The National Supermarket Association claims the Hunts Point store would affect about 20 nearby grocers, while the East Harlem location could affect 26 businesses.

The lawsuit is the second challenging the municipal grocery store initiative. The Multicultural Business Coalition, which represents small grocers and bodega owners, filed a class action in Manhattan Supreme Court in August, raising similar concerns about the planâs effects on competitors.

Speaking with Andrew Ross Sorkin at the DealBook Summit earlier this week, Mamdani compared the cityâs subsidized grocery stores to public services like the âsubway or a public school or a library or sanitation.â

âThe reason we are doing this is because what we are seeing is the lines of New Yorkers at food pantries are just continuing to lengthen every single day,â the mayor said. âItâs not a Covid-specific phenomenon. And we need to make it easier for them to actually be able to afford.â

âWe have determined this is necessary,â he added. “And when I think about what is necessary for a dignified life in New York City and anywhere, frankly, it is very easy to come back to food because you cannot live without it.â

#7722. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7721. NYC Mayor Mamdani plans to close Rikers Island jail by 2032

The first borough-based jails, under construction in Brooklyn, are set to open in 2029.

MANHATTAN (CN) âÂ New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday announced a new plan to close the notoriously dangerous jail complex on Rikers Island by 2032 by dramatically reducing the number of people imprisoned in the city’s system and moving detainees to smaller, more modern facilities.

“The call to close Rikers has echoed across our city for decades. Work has begun to do so, then stopped, then started once again. What will make this chapter different is our commitment to see it through,â Mamdani said at a City Hall press conference Friday.

The New York City Council voted in 2019, under former Mayor Bill de Blasio, to close Rikers by Aug. 31, 2027. But meeting that deadline is widely considered impossible, particularly after delays under former Mayor Eric Adams, who opposed the borough-based jails being built to replace Rikers.

Mamdani aims to reduce the daily jail population from 6,600 to 4,100 through alternatives to detention, programs to reduce recidivism and efforts to reduce court delays.

Mamdaniâs administration developed the plan with a court-appointed special monitor selected earlier this year. In May 2025, a federal judge ordered Rikers placed under an independent receiver, finding that “the level of unconstitutional danger has not improved for the people who live and work in the jails is both alarming and unacceptable.â

“It is an extensive, rigorous plan,” said Mamdani, who appeared at on crutches at Friday’s announcement, explaining that he had torn his Achilles tendon during a friendly soccer match against members of the press on Thursday night. He’ll be in a boot for six to eight weeks.

The first borough-based jail, under construction in Brooklyn, is set to open in 2029, followed by facilities in Queens and the Bronx in 2031 and Manhattan in 2032. New York City Council will have to approve the deadlines.

“These jails will look, feel and most importantly operate very differently than Rikers,” Mamdani said.

Rikers has become notorious for filthy conditions, deteriorating facilities and understaffing that contribute to widespread violence, injuries and illness. Five people have died in its jails in 2026 alone.

Better access to public transit would ease family visits, while jail reform advocates say keeping detainees connected to their communities and courts is essential to fair proceedings and successful reentry. Most people held at Rikers are awaiting trial.

“Any family member of someone held at Rikers will tell you how isolating that jail is. How it can take hours to visit a loved one. How far away you feel from the rest of the city,” Mamdani said.

Mamdaniâs office said reducing the jail population by thousands would also benefit correction officers, who have long raised concerns about understaffing.

Correction Officersâ Benevolent Association President Benny Boscio said Friday the plan was the first in the effort to close Rikers to emphasize officersâ safety and working conditions.

“Prioritizing our members’ safety and working conditions is central to both our advocacy and the future success of our jails,” he said.

Boscio welcomed the cityâs commitment to repairing broken cell doors but called its plan to reduce available jail beds “ill-conceived” and “irresponsible,” arguing that incarcerating fewer people would jeopardize public safety.

“If you cannot put a ceiling on the violent crime committed against New Yorkers, then you cannot responsibly cap the maximum capacity of our jail population,” the association said.

The advocacy group Campaign to Close Rikers, led by former detainees and family members of those incarcerated in NYC jails, said it was excited to see the plan unveiled.

âInaction and obstruction by the previous administration created serious delays in closing Rikers that came with staggering human and financial costs, including dozens of New Yorkers who died behind bars while awaiting their day in court, and thousands of others in need of housing and treatment who instead remained trapped in a relentless cycle of incarceration and instability," the group said in a statement.

The organization urged officials to “act with urgency” to close at least one more jail in the Rikers complex by August 2027, which would mark the shuttering of half the jails on the island by the initial deadline.

The Campaign to Close Rikers also said the city should be sending fewer people into the court system in the first place.

“We can do that by ending the criminalization of poverty that is carried out through mass low-level arrests in response to social and economic challenges that police ultimately cannot solve,” the group said.

#7716. 2026 Year in Review: When AI dominated the room

I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to new technology faster than ever before. At the same time, technology has advanced exponentially, with artificial intelligence changing how information is obtained and how work gets done.

At record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors. Meanwhile, AI startups proliferated across the legal technology landscape, with some disappearing overnight, while others were snapped up and acquired less than a year after launch.

It was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up. From tracking updated software features and emerging AI-powered technologies to learning how to use AI ethically, lawyers had a lot on their plates. That’s where my 2026 columns came in. Each one offered a summary of the latest legal technology news or provided roadmaps for legal software adoption in law firms.

Trusts and estates lawyers rely on drafting software to create complex planning documents and manage related estate work. These tools include features like guided interviews, automated forms and shared client information that support document creation and reduce drafting errors. Some software also helps lawyers customize plans and handle tasks such as trust funding and estate administration. Understanding how the options differ can assist lawyers in choosing the software that fits their trusts and estates practice’s workflows.

AI systems reflect the assumptions and perspectives of the people who develop them, as well as the data used to train them. Those assumptions can shape AI outputs and reinforce bias, especially when women and other underrepresented groups have little input into how systems are designed. Drawing on the Women + AI Summit, including more perspectives when developing AI matters; it can impact the questions considered, improve outcomes, and determine how these systems affect users and the public at large.

At Legalweek 2026, agentic AI and the competition to become law firms’ central AI platform were recurring themes. There were also plenty of updates from legal technology providers, from platforms that connected research, drafting and firm data to specialized tools for e-discovery, litigation, legal research and skills training. The conference announcements highlight how companies are building both integrated ecosystems and focused applications that help lawyers incorporate new AI-driven workflows into their firms.

Drawing on findings from the 8am 2026 Legal Industry Report, this column examines how the profession is responding to rapid AI adoption, access-to-justice hurdles and concerns about the rule of law. The report shows that individual AI use has grown faster than the implementation of firm policies and training, even as survey respondents see technology as one way of bridging the access-to-justice moat. Also notable was that lawyers were most concerned about the rule of law and its continued degradation.

The growing number of court filings with fabricated or inaccurate case citations has led to a new category of tools designed to check AI-generated legal documents. Citation checkers can help identify false citations, misquoted language and inaccurate descriptions of case holdings. There are citation-checking tools built into drafting platforms in addition to those found in stand-alone applications, with a focus on their capabilities and costs. Before investing in a new tool, consider whether the time saved through AI research, drafting and citation checking justifies the expense or whether traditional research and drafting may ultimately be more cost-effective.

As AI takes on routine work traditionally assigned to junior lawyers, it may also reduce opportunities to develop practical legal skills. Training platforms can allow law students and early-career lawyers to build experience through courtroom simulations, interactive exercises and AI- or VR-based practice. These tools allow users to rehearse tasks, such as deposition questioning, negotiation and courtroom advocacy, with some offering immediate performance feedback. Using these simulation-based learning platforms, recent law school graduates are better able to bridge the experiential gap and ensure that they have the building blocks needed to thrive in the AI era.

Partnerships and integrations dominated the news at ILTACON 2026, as legal technology companies worked to connect their AI tools with legal data, software and workflows. In addition to those developments, there were new products that streamlined litigation, legal writing and law firm pricing. The conference takeaway was that legal AI is moving beyond stand-alone tools toward connected systems, for better or for worse.

Litigation teams often work with large, complex collections of digital evidence, which can be difficult to organize and analyze using traditional methods. AI-powered fact analysis tools can assist with the review of case materials by identifying people, events and inconsistencies and by creating timelines that link to supporting documents. These tools can help litigators analyze and understand the evidence and collaborate more efficiently with their teams.

As new AI-powered platforms enter the market, solo and small-firm lawyers now have more affordable options for legal research. There are some tools priced at $100 or less per month that lawyers can use to quickly and easily search caselaw and statutes. Some also offer case analysis and citation-checking tools to confirm subsequent case treatment. These platforms provide smaller practices with more options, but lawyers should still weigh the cost and accuracy rates against existing research tools, along with the time required to verify AI-generated results.

Nicole Black is a Rochester, New York-based attorney, author and journalist. She is the principal legal insight strategist at 8am, parent company of LawPay, MyCase, CasePeer and DocketWise. She is the nationally recognized author of Cloud Computing for Lawyers and is a co-author of Social Media for Lawyers: The Next Frontier, both published by the American Bar Association. She writes regular columns for ABAJournal.com and Above the Law, has authored hundreds of articles for other publications, and she regularly speaks at conferences regarding the intersection of law and emerging technologies. Follow her on LinkedIn, or she can be reached at [email protected].

This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

#7715. Reinsurer TIG found liable over Libby Mine asbestos exposure claims

Omaha-based National Indemnity sued, saying the reinsurer did not fully cover its losses after Montana failed to warn of the dangers in and around the small city of Libby.

OMAHA, Neb. (CN) â An eight-person federal jury found reinsurer TIG liable after Omaha-based National Indemnity claimed TIG didn’t fully cover a sweeping payout for widespread contamination from the Libby Mine asbestos exposure.

Jurors found National Indemnity complied with its obligations under the reinsurance certificate and proved its breach of contract claim against TIG. They awarded National Indemnity $39.2 million in indemnity, $3.2 million in prejudgment interest, $21.1 million in postjudgment interest and $16.1 million in expenses.

They declined to award National Indemnity any future defense costs.

Attorneys for both sides declined to comment after the verdict was read.

National Indemnity Insurance Company turned to TIG Insurance Company and other reinsurers after agreeing in 2022, with Montana, to resolve all coverage claims over asbestos exposure from the mine since the 1960s for $157 million.

National Indemnity insured the state from July 1, 1973, to July 1, 1975; TIG provided the company’s reinsurance at that time.

TIG claimed National Indemnity did not offer adequate evidence and billed amounts not covered by the reinsurance agreement, essentially finagling the numbers to make TIG cover part of the massive bill.

âIt lied," said Scott L. Davis, a Dallas-based attorney for the Spencer Fane firm, representing TIG, speaking of National Indemnity during closing arguments late Thursday afternoon.

National Indemnity said it kept TIG informed throughout the claims process, but the reinsurer never got involved, something it had a right to do.

“They could have helped; they didnât,” Michael Knoerzer, a New York-based attorney for Clyde & Co., representing National Indemnity, told the jury Thursday. âItâs undisputed in this case they never asked.â

In 2004, the state of Montana was found liable for asbestos risk to miners and residents near Libby, a small city in the state’s northwest.

From 1963 to 1990, W.R. Grace & Co. extracted vermiculite at the mine, about 7 miles outside of Libby. Vermiculite, once commonly used for fireproof roofing, insulation and wallpaper, is not dangerous. But the asbestos the mining stirred up was.

Decades of widespread asbestos contamination from the mine caused the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to declare its first-ever public health emergency during a 2009 Superfund cleanup.

Thousands of W.R. Grace workers, their families and residents since the 1960s have been injured or died from lung disease related to working at or living near the mine.

The fight over who should be held liable started about 2000, shortly after reports of workers falling ill sparked an emergency cleanup. Contamination has since been blamed for hundreds of deaths.

Reinsurance is dubbed âinsurance for insurance companiesâ by the Reinsurance Association of America. Under reinsurance, one insurance company indemnifies another for a loss the company buying the policy cannot handle alone â something that National Indemnity claims TIG did not fully do.

After the $157 million payout, National Indemnity billed its reinsurers more than $101 million. They did not pay. Since first filing the lawsuit in 2022, all other reinsurers except TIG have been dropped from the suit. TIG has paid National Indemnity what it believed it owed â $12.7 million.

According to National Indemnity, the insurance contract required National Indemnity to pay as much as $3 million per loss, with unlimited occurrences. At first, the state said 21 occurrences involved state inspectors not warning miners about the asbestos risk.

But National Indemnity feared that, with potentially thousands of miners and locals affected by asbestos exposure, the number of occurrences could multiply as the matter moved again through Montana courts, with the state Supreme Court telling the parties to litigate the number of occurrences.

Ultimately, National Indemnity and the state settled at 27 occurrences. At $3 million apiece, the bill came to $81 million. The roughly $76 million remaining largely came from past and present defense costs.

Under their contract, TIG was responsible for one-third of National Indemnityâs costs. So, according to National Indemnity, it would have to pay $1 million for each occurrence.

Montana and National Indemnity counted each failure to warn by the state as an occurrence. At issue is whether individual deaths could also count as an occurrence. National Indemnity argued it could have found itself on the hook for âbillionsâ if individual deaths were counted, which led it to settle at 27.

In her instructions to the jury Thursday, U.S. District Judge Susan M. Bazis said National Indemnity would have to prove, by greater weight of evidence, that it performed its obligation under the contract and that TIG breached it, causing damages to the Omaha-based insurer.

The Joe Biden appointee said TIG agreed there was adequate proof of 21 occurrences. National Indemnity would have to prove it provided satisfactory evidence of each occurrence to TIG.

“By greater weight of the evidence” is a less strict standard than the “beyond a reasonable doubt” standard in criminal cases. As in criminal cases, the jury selects a foreperson, and the vote must be unanimous.
